q: You hear a MAYDAY on 16 from a yacht you cannot see. What do you do first?
a: Listen, write it down, wait for the coast station
o: Answer at once to say you heard her
Change channel to keep 16 clear
Call her back to ask for her position
why: First listen and record: a coast station normally acknowledges and coordinates.

q: You can reach the sinking yacht in half an hour. What do you do on the radio?
a: Acknowledge, then tell the coastguard you are going
o: Keep listening — only coast stations acknowledge
Send a MAYDAY RELAY and keep your course
Head there in silence to keep 16 clear
why: If no coast station answers and you can help, acknowledge the MAYDAY and inform the coastguard.

q: You, on yacht Aura, acknowledge a MAYDAY from yacht Thalassa. Which form is right?
a: MAYDAY, Thalassa ×3, THIS IS, Aura ×3, RECEIVED MAYDAY
o: Thalassa, THIS IS Aura, ROGER your message, OVER
RECEIVED MAYDAY, with no names given at all
SEELONCE MAYDAY, Thalassa, THIS IS Aura
why: Acknowledgement: MAYDAY, the casualty's name ×3, THIS IS, your name ×3, RECEIVED MAYDAY.

q: During a rescue you hear the station controlling it say "SEELONCE MAYDAY". What does it require of you?
a: Keep off the channel unless you are in the rescue
o: Use low power for any routine calls
Switch your radio off until morning
Repeat it so that more boats hear it
why: SEELONCE MAYDAY imposes silence: only stations taking part in the distress may transmit.

q: You have kept quiet on 16 all afternoon during a rescue. Now you hear "SEELONCE FEENEE". What has changed?
a: Distress traffic is over; normal use resumes
o: Only short, essential calls are allowed
The silence is extended for another hour
A second distress has begun nearby
why: SEELONCE FEENEE lifts radio silence: the distress traffic is over.

q: During a rescue you have kept off 16. Now the station controlling the distress traffic announces "PRUDONCE". What does it tell you?
a: The distress is not over, but restricted working may resume
o: The distress is over and normal working resumes
Total silence on 16 until further notice
Only the vessel in distress may transmit
why: PRUDONCE: restricted working may resume; full normal working comes only with SEELONCE FEENEE.

q: You normally reach your friend on 16 first. With this going on, how do you get your message to her?
a: Leave 16 alone: wait, or reach her another way
o: Call quickly between the distress messages
Call on 16 on low power so nobody minds
Call her by voice on channel 70 instead
why: No routine traffic on a channel carrying distress working: wait, or find another way.

fig.title: On channel 16
lines: You want to tell a friend's yacht
that you will be late for dinner

q: A yacht's MAYDAY has been acknowledged and a search begins. Who coordinates it?
a: The coastguard's rescue centre (MRCC)
o: The first yacht to reach the scene
The yacht that sent the MAYDAY
The office of the nearest marina
why: Search and rescue is coordinated by the MRCC, usually through a coast station.

q: You are searching with other yachts, and the coastguard tells everyone on scene to work on channel 6. What do you do?
a: Use 6 for search talk, as directed
o: Stay on 16 — distress talk never leaves it
Pick your own quiet channel with the lifeboat
Use channel 70 so the talk goes by DSC
why: On-scene talk uses the channel the coordinator directs, often 16 or 6.

q: You hear a MAYDAY and reach for the log book. What do you write down?
a: Name, position, problem, help needed, persons, time
o: Only the name of the vessel in distress
Only the channel and the time you heard it
Nothing — the coast station records it all
why: Note everything: you may have to relay it or help, and the coast station may not have heard.

q: A helicopter lowers its winch wire towards your cockpit. What must happen before anyone touches it?
a: It touches the water or deck first, to earth it
o: Someone ties it to a cleat to hold it steady
The crew turns the VHF off to avoid sparks
The engine stops so the boat lies still
why: The wire carries a static charge: let it earth on the sea or deck first, and never tie it to the boat.

q: A rescue helicopter is hovering overhead and the noise is deafening. How do you get its instructions?
a: Listen on VHF and do what the crew tells you
o: Shout up to the winchman as he comes down
Wait for a written note sent down the wire
By hand signals only — VHF is not used
why: Helicopter crews brief the yacht by VHF; follow their instructions exactly.

q: The helicopter will arrive in ten minutes. How do you prepare the deck?
a: Stow or lash down loose gear, clear a space
o: Hoist every sail so you are easy to see
Keep all crew on deck to catch the wire
Leave it — the downdraft will clear it
why: Downdraft blows loose gear into the rotor and wire: secure everything and clear the pick-up area.

fig.title: Helicopter on its way
lines: To lift an injured crew member

q: You are much too far away to help this vessel. What do you do on the radio?
a: Keep listening and noting, but stay silent
o: Acknowledge too, so she knows you heard
Send a MAYDAY RELAY to make sure
Call her and offer your position
why: Once a coast station has it, distant yachts keep quiet and listen — they may be asked to help later.

q: You are close and could help the burning yacht. What do you do on the radio?
a: Offer help to the coast station, with your position
o: Nothing — the coast station has it in hand
Acknowledge the burning yacht's MAYDAY yourself
Head there without a word to keep 16 clear
why: Offer your help to the station controlling the distress, with your position and ETA.

fig.title: MAYDAY nearby
lines: You can be there in 20 minutes

q: Radio silence has been imposed, yet the rescue centre is calling you. May you answer?
a: Yes — you are part of the distress traffic
o: No — SEELONCE MAYDAY silences everyone
Only after SEELONCE FEENEE is given
Only on channel 6, never on 16
why: Radio silence binds stations not involved; those taking part in the rescue keep talking.

fig.title: Silence imposed
lines: You are the yacht nearest the casualty
The MRCC calls you by name on 16

q: During a long rescue you hear three signals over several hours. In which order do they normally come?
a: SEELONCE MAYDAY, PRUDONCE, SEELONCE FEENEE
o: PRUDONCE, SEELONCE MAYDAY, SEELONCE FEENEE
SEELONCE FEENEE, PRUDONCE, SEELONCE MAYDAY
SEELONCE MAYDAY, SEELONCE FEENEE, PRUDONCE
why: Silence imposed, then restricted working allowed, then silence lifted.

q: You might have found what everyone is looking for. What do you do on the radio?
a: Report it to the coordinator on the channel in use
o: Send a new MAYDAY for the person in the water
Wait until you are sure before saying anything
Put out a SÉCURITÉ to all stations on 16
why: Report sightings at once to whoever coordinates the search, on the channel they set.

fig.title: Searching
lines: Looking for a yacht's crew overboard
The MRCC gave you a search area
Something orange in the water ahead

q: You are heading to help a yacht in distress. The coastguard calls to say a lifeboat is there and you are not needed. What do you do?
a: Acknowledge the message and resume your passage
o: Carry on anyway in case they need you
Ignore it — you already said you were going
Ask for SEELONCE FEENEE before you turn
why: Acknowledge your release by the coordinator; your help is no longer needed.

q: The lifeboat cannot hear the yacht in distress, but you hear both. The MRCC asks you to pass messages between them. How?
a: Pass each message on exactly as you heard it
o: Shorten them in your own words to save time
Refuse — only coast stations may relay
Tell the yacht to shout louder into her set
why: When relaying, pass messages on accurately and in full — the coordinator relies on them.
